questions.stem: What runs along the modern periodic table's left-to-right order?

options.explanation: Every step along the table adds one proton, which is what atomic number counts.
Mass-based ordering was the older idea; the modern table follows proton count.
Discovery order would scatter similar elements; the table orders by structure.
Names are labels, not the organising principle.

questions.stem: How does an element's proton count compare with its left-hand neighbour's?

options.explanation: Adjacent elements differ by a single proton, which is why the order is so regular.
Eight is a period-length idea, not the neighbour-to-neighbour step.
Doubling would tear through the sequence; the step is one.
The pattern is as fixed as it gets: plus one every step.

questions.stem: Why is the table ordered by atomic number rather than by something else?

options.text: So that elements with similar properties end up in the same columns
options.explanation: The arrangement is functional: chemical families gather vertically.

options.text: Because atomic numbers are easier to spell
options.explanation: The choice is chemical, not cosmetic.

options.text: Because proton counts can change during reactions
options.explanation: Proton counts are fixed; that stability is precisely why they can anchor the table.

options.text: So the table fits neatly on one page
options.explanation: Page layout has nothing to do with it; property patterns do.

questions.stem: In a reaction an atom gains electrons. Which number is unchanged?

options.explanation: Electron changes cannot touch the proton count, so the element keeps its identity.
That is exactly what changed when the electron was gained.
Gaining an electron alters the charge by definition.

options.text: None - gaining an electron makes a new element
options.explanation: Only a change in proton count makes a new element; electrons merely make ions.

questions.stem: Where do elements with similar chemical properties end up in the table?

options.explanation: Similar properties sharing a column is the payoff of the atomic-number ordering.
Rows collect neighbours in proton count, not chemical look-alikes.
No diagonal rule governs the basic arrangement.
The whole design exists to keep chemical families together.

questions.stem: Which description matches the table's rows and columns?

options.text: Periods are rows; groups are columns
options.explanation: The vocabulary is fixed: periods across, groups down.

options.text: Periods are columns; groups are rows
options.explanation: The two names are swapped; remember groups go down like gravity.

options.text: Both rows and columns are called groups
options.explanation: Only the vertical columns carry the name group.

options.text: Neither direction has a special name
options.explanation: Both directions are named because both carry information.

questions.stem: What does the period number tell you about an atom?

options.text: How many shells of electrons it holds
options.explanation: Period 3 atoms have three shells; the row number is the shell count.

options.text: How many electrons are in the outer shell
options.explanation: That is the group number's job, not the period's.
Proton count is the atomic number, read from order rather than position name.
Neutrons vary between isotopes and appear nowhere in the position numbers.

questions.stem: What does the group number tell you about an atom?

options.text: How many electrons sit in its outermost shell
options.explanation: Group 4 atoms carry four outer electrons; the column is the outer count.
Shell count comes from the period row, not the group column.

options.text: How many isotopes the element has
options.explanation: Isotope counts are properties of samples and discovery, not of position.
Atomic mass is a separate number printed in the element's box.

questions.stem: Which numbering does the table use for its columns?

options.text: 1 to 7, then a final column called Group 0
options.explanation: The last column is named 0 instead of 8 - a naming convention of the table.
The leftmost column is Group 1; the 0 belongs to the far right.
The final column deliberately breaks the run and is called Group 0.
This course numbers the groups; letters belong to other table styles.

questions.stem: An atom has 3 shells and 5 electrons in its outermost. Where does it sit?

options.explanation: Shell count sets the period, outer-electron count sets the group.
The two translations are swapped; shells give the period.
Group 0 is the last column's name, not a home for five outer electrons.
Periods run only 1 to 7; three shells means Period 3.
